response:
Well, that’s a pretty well-known story.  But there’s actually more to it than that.  Thanksgiving has its roots in the Wampanoongas, a Native American tribe that lived along the Atlantic coast from Massachusetts to South Carolina.  The Wampanoongas had their own Thanksgiving celebrations, which involved dancing around a large turn-of-the-century stove with gifts.  The turn-of-the-century stove had two doors–one opened to the fire and the other to food.  At the end of the dance, the door that lead to the food would be locked to prevent the food from being stolen. 
On Thanksgiving, the Wampanoongas held a feast for their tribe, including turkeys.  The tradition stayed with them for many years and gradually spread to other parts of New England.  
By the mid-1800s, Thanksgiving celebrated on the fourth Thursday of November had become the tradition for North America.  But in the mid-1800s, when the turkey was first introduced into Thanksgiving celebrations in North America, turkeys were not popular among the Wampanoongas.  They preferred roasted fowl and never ate wild turkey.  
One Thanksgiving in 1863, George Ross and his Thanksgiving turkey survived slaughter and was taken to the governor’s office to serve as a Thanksgiving dinner present for the governor.  
Afterwards, George Ross was celebrated all over the northeastern U.S., and was even included in an article in “The Atlantic Monthly” in May 1864.  George Ross had gained the title of America’s first turkey.  
As Thanksgiving celebrations became more popular and turkey became more widely eaten, the Wampanoongas felt the need to take back the Thanksgiving turkey.  In 1874, George Ross was invited to speak at a Thanksgiving celebration in Albany, New York.  Ross’ speech, “Thanksgiving and the Origin of a Food,” addressed the question of whether turkey should still be referred to as Thanksgiving turkey.  He responded that, in this day and age where turkey was more of a national food and not a “Native American food,” turkey would probably be better served as the national Thanksgiving bird.  His talk, “The Thanksgiving Turkey and the Native American Food Problem,” was published in “The Atlantic Monthly” in August 1874.

prompt: Human: Who sets the price of postage at the USPS?
response:
The US Postal Service (USPS或USPSteps.com) sets the price of postage, which is what you pay for each stamp you buy. It is called the “Per-Postage-Price” or “PP” in short, and it does change on a periodic basis, every six months or so. When it does change, you’ll see a new date on the postage stamp that shows when you purchase the stamp. You don’t need to buy a new stamp every time, it’s only necessary for the change to happen once every six months.

When you purchase stamps you are buying time in the economy of numbers. So if you buy a large block of stamps, the USPS knows they’ll be using them for many months, so they can set the prices accordingly. There are four classes of postage stamps, or denominations.  They are:

First-class letters are for standard letters. This is the basic class of mail for personal and business mail.  They come in four denominations, two 1¾-ounce (5 grams) and two 3½-ounce (18 grams). A 1/4-ounce stamp (3 grams) is also included.  They have a standard blue design. 

Second-class letters come in one denomination, the 1-ounce (30 grams) 4-stars-stamp. 
Third-class letters are for all other standard mail, including commercial packages, newspaper and magazine shipments, and business mail.  For this class of mail you can choose from two denominations: one nickel and one dime. 

Fourth-class letters are for first-class letters, the most valuable class, except that if you send a package or a large box of things in the package, the postage goes up by a factor of ten and it becomes a first-class postage stamp. 
Fifth-class letters are for the most expensive types of first-class mail: parcels, large commercial packages, heavy weight boxes.  They have both a half-dollar (50-grams) and a dime (10 grams) stamp. 
Sixth-class letters are for the most costly mail of the first-class class, such as newspapers.  They have four 3-ounce (100 grams) stamps, two half-dollars, and one dime. 

The last class of postage stamps are for all other standard letters (letters below first-class), like bills of exchange, international letters, and legal correspondence.  The last class includes an express stamp, a heavy first-class stamp, international stamps, and legal correspondence stamps. 
Postal Rates are calculated by multiplying the sum of all postal rates by the number of pounds of mail sent.  The sum is calculated by adding the postage for each class of mail.  
As a rule of thumb, it’s best to use the first class stamp most of the time.  
The last rate adjustment was made on December 31, 2008.  Since then the USPS has not made any rate adjustments, unless you specifically ask for them.
